sections: A market morning or a design-shop afternoon

Puducherry offers several different shopping trips. Goubert Market is a working market; MG Road has a Sunday market; the French Quarter has small clothing and design shops; Auroville offers products from its own makers. Pick the kind of browse you want rather than treating all four as one continuous walk. Check the current shop address and opening arrangements before travelling.
Goubert Market and the Sunday market

Incredible India identifies Goubert Market with produce, spices and everyday market activity, and the Sunday market on MG Road with clothing, accessories and small goods. These are useful choices when you want a bazaar rather than a curated boutique. Ask before photographing people at work, keep loading routes clear and compare the object itself. A market setting does not establish that an item is handmade or locally produced.
Naushad Ali and Chintz: two fashion leads

A 2024 Condé Nast Traveller report identifies Naushad Ali on Surcouf Street for clothing in fabrics including cotton, linen and silk, and Chintz as a multi-designer store. They offer different starting points: a designer collection or a wider edit. Use the report to find a lead, then confirm the current location and collection. Look at fabric composition, fit and care instructions rather than assuming every piece shares one sustainability claim.
Janaki and Galerie Surcouf: objects as well as clothing

The same independent report describes Janaki as a place to investigate Auroville clothing, ceramics and fragrance products, and Galerie Surcouf for ceramics, books and home objects. Choose one material or use before browsing. Ask who made a ceramic piece, whether it is intended for food use, and how a fragile purchase will be packed. A gallery-like setting does not make every object an antique or an original artwork.
Cluny Embroidery Centre: look closely at the work

Both national tourism information and the independent shopping report identify Cluny Embroidery Centre as a lead for embroidered household linen. This is a different purchase from a printed souvenir cloth. Ask about the fabric, embroidery technique and washing instructions, and inspect the reverse as well as the front. Confirm visiting arrangements before setting out; do not assume production spaces are open for an unannounced tour.
Auroville Visitors Centre: a separate outing

Auroville's own Visitors Centre page lists boutiques including La Boutique d'Auroville, Mirra and Kalki, with products such as clothing, tableware, jewellery, incense and furnishings. This is a practical starting point when you want to compare Auroville-made goods in one area. Keep the journey separate from a short French Quarter walk. A shopping visit is not access to the interior of the Matrimandir; those visitor arrangements are a different question.
Buy for the journey home

For linen, ask about laundering and colour care. For ceramics, agree on protective packing before paying. For oils, cosmetics or food, check the label and the rules that apply to your flight and destination. Keep a receipt that names the item and seller. Old travel reports are shopping leads, not proof of current stock, opening hours or prices.

sections: Shop with the port city in mind

Mattancherry makes more sense when you remember that trade is part of the place, not a theme added for tourists. Spice warehouses and shops sit within a neighbourhood shaped by different communities and long connections across the sea. A good shopping walk can reveal some of that history without turning every stop into a purchase. Start with a short list: spices for your kitchen, a small piece of art, or a gift that travels well. Those are different errands. A stall full of attractive objects may be enjoyable to browse without being the right place to verify a textile, an antique or the origin of a handmade piece.
Let the spices be the first conversation

Pepper, cardamom, cloves and cinnamon are useful starting points in Mattancherry. Compare small quantities before buying a large mixed hamper. Ask what is in the packet, where it was packed and how to store it. Whole spices can be easier to assess than a blend whose ingredients are unclear. Smell and appearance are useful clues, not a certification of quality. Prefer clear labels and clean, intact packaging. A simple packet of something you regularly cook with can be a better purchase than an impressive box you do not know how to use. Ask about the intended use if a spice is unfamiliar, and avoid treating a seller's health claims as medical advice.
Understand the two kinds of street activity

The spice lanes are also working spaces. Keep doorways and loading areas clear, and ask before entering a warehouse or photographing workers. Watch the sorting, packing and movement of goods from a respectful distance. Retail browsing and commercial handling are not the same invitation. Nearby Jew Street is known for antique shops, spice stalls and galleries. Allow time to look, but do not confuse an antique-style object with a documented antique. If age or provenance affects the price, ask for written information rather than relying on a story told across the counter.
Buy art and objects for reasons you can explain

For a small artwork or handmade gift, ask who made it and what material it uses. A direct answer helps you decide whether the piece is genuinely connected to your visit or simply a widely sold souvenir. Check the object itself: finish, joints, edges and whether anything is likely to break in a bag. Be especially cautious with old-looking objects, religious pieces or items made from unfamiliar natural materials. Export and import rules depend on the item and your destination. Check the relevant official rules before buying something whose age, material or status is uncertain. A shop saying it is fine to travel with is not the same as clearance at a border.
Finish the purchase, not just the browsing

Confirm the total, the quantity and what the receipt describes. Photograph a fragile object before it is packed and ask for protection that will survive the rest of your journey. For food, check the destination's rules on spices and other agricultural products, and keep labels where they can be inspected. If you want Kerala textiles, give that a separate search with clear questions about fibre, weave and origin. This walk is not a claim that every souvenir shop is a specialist cloth seller. Leave with a few things you understand and will use. The best reminder of Kochi may be pepper in a meal months later, alongside a memory of the streets where you chose it.
Kairali or Surabhi: use the institutional lead, then check the piece

Kerala Tourism names Kairali and Surabhi among handicraft shopping leads in the Kochi area. The Handicrafts Development Corporation of Kerala describes Kairali as its showroom brand and its role in marketing artisan work. Those are useful starting points when you want to ask about making rather than only compare decorative objects. Confirm the current outlet location and opening before going. Ask what the actual piece is made from, who made it and what care it needs. An institution's general purpose does not establish every item's origin, material or price. Inspect the object that will be packed and retain the bill.
Textiles: choose the cloth and the form separately

Hantex's Ernakulam-region directory lists an Ernakulam Emporium in the Hantex Building near the Boat Jetty. That provides a specific textile-shopping lead, distinct from a Fort Kochi sightseeing stop. Check the current showroom and collection before making a special journey. For a saree, home textile or garment, ask about fibre, dimensions and care. If a purchase depends on handloom production, ask about that particular cloth. A cream surface or gold-toned border is not by itself proof of the weave or the border's material. Confirm any blouse piece, stitching, lining and alteration cost separately.
Mattancherry: browse trade and craft without inventing provenance

Kerala Tourism identifies Mattancherry as a place to browse spices, wooden objects, jewellery and traditional crafts. Crafters, in its own account, locates its business in Jew Town and describes a history involving antiques and architectural pieces. That is a shop's account of its business, not independent authentication of an object offered for sale. An old-looking finish, a dealer's narrative or a neighbourhood's history does not prove age or lawful export. Ask for written provenance and specialist advice before an important antique purchase. A reproduction can still be appealing when sold clearly as a reproduction; do not pay an antique premium for an unanswered claim.
Wood and coir: inspect the useful details

For a basket or small box, examine the base, handles, hinges and finish. Ask about material and intended use rather than assuming every natural-looking object is locally made. Check whether a decorative vessel is meant to hold food; the answer should come from the maker or seller, not its attractive shape. A large carved piece creates a different commitment from a small keepsake. Before agreeing to shipping, get the packing, delivery, damage and return terms in writing and check destination restrictions for its material. When those answers are unclear, choose a smaller well-understood object or leave without buying.
Crafters and Lawrence: named Jew Town leads

Kerala Tourism's handicraft directory lists Crafters in Jew Town and Lawrence Handicrafts and Exports on Synagogue Lane. These are specific leads for a craft-and-object browse rather than another spice packet. Check their current location and opening arrangements before visiting. Ask about material, maker, age and shipping separately. A tourism-directory listing does not authenticate the age of an object offered for sale.
An antique claim needs more than a story

Kerala Tourism describes Jew Town shops displaying wooden carvings, oil lamps, spice boxes, photographs and ceramic objects. Those categories explain why the walk is interesting; they do not establish the age or lawful export status of an individual piece. If the appeal depends on an antique claim, obtain written provenance and current export guidance before committing. A newly made craft object can be a better souvenir when the history cannot be checked.

sections: Two shopping areas, two starting points

Commercial Street and Chickpet offer different ways to shop in Bengaluru. Commercial Street and its side lanes bring clothing, footwear, accessories and fabrics into a varied browse. Chickpet is a stronger starting point when textiles, saris or silk are the reason for going. Choose the purpose before arranging a long cross-city shopping day. Neither area is a promise of the lowest price or a particular item being in stock. Shops change, and even a well-known market can be the wrong place for your needs. Decide what you want to compare and what you can carry home. One thoughtful purchase can be enough for an afternoon.
Commercial Street: look into the side lanes

The main stretch gives clothing and shoe shops a visible place, while the side lanes add fabric stores and smaller accessory shops. A short detour can change the character of the browse. Keep your route small enough to return to a shop you liked rather than wandering until every display starts to look the same. Try clothing where permitted and look at seams, fastening and fit, not only the way it hangs on a rack. Check footwear on both feet and ask whether the displayed pair is the one you will receive. For accessories, compare the material and finish. A modest item can still deserve a careful look if you expect to use it often.
Chickpet: arrive with a textile question

Chickpet's narrow lanes and textile shops suit an outing with a clearer aim. If you want a sari, decide whether you are looking for something light for everyday use or a more elaborate piece for an occasion. If it is a gift, think about the recipient's preferences before the display decides for you. Ask what the fabric is, how it should be cared for and whether the price includes any finishing. Do not infer silk content from sheen alone. A seller's regional or weaving label is a claim to understand, not independent proof of origin. Where authenticity matters, ask for written product details and buy from a shop whose information you can check.
The useful comparison is like with like

A bargain becomes hard to judge when two items differ in fibre, size or finish. Compare similar pieces before deciding that one shop is cheaper. Look at the reverse of a fabric, the edges and any uneven work. For dress material, confirm the length and what separate pieces are included. Bargaining may be part of some transactions, but fixed-price shops also exist. Ask rather than assume. Keep the conversation respectful and stop when the price no longer suits you. An agreed price should cover the item you inspected; substitutions, extra finishing and delivery should be clear before payment.
Leave with an item, not an unfinished errand

If tailoring is needed, confirm measurements, collection date and what happens if an adjustment is required. Do not arrange work against the last hours of your trip unless the timing is dependable. A ready-to-wear piece may be the better choice when you cannot return to collect something. Check the return policy before paying, keep the receipt and confirm the merchant name and amount. Agree on a pickup point outside the most crowded stretch when arranging transport. Avoid publishing a purchase as handmade or locally woven unless you have evidence for that description. A successful Bengaluru shopping walk leaves you with something that fits your life, not a story about a deal you cannot explain.
Cauvery Emporium: a Karnataka craft direction

The Bengaluru Urban district tourism page identifies Cauvery Emporium as a Karnataka State Handicrafts Development Corporation outlet for traditional Karnataka crafts. This adds a specific craft-shopping direction beyond Commercial Street clothing and Chickpet textiles. Check the current branch and ask what material and craft tradition an item represents. Do not assume that every decorative object is sandalwood or that a familiar outlet name replaces an itemised bill.
sources: Bengaluru Urban district: shopping and Cauvery Emporium
